Metal activity series

Metals differ in how readily they lose electrons and become positive ions. You can see it on a lab bench: a reactive metal fizzes in water or dilute acid, burns brightly in oxygen and pushes a less reactive metal out of a solution of its ions. No single test separates every metal, but stacking the results from several tests builds an activity series that you can check against the standard series in a data book. in the wild

Chemistry in water works like a power bank charging a phone.

Almost everything that happens in water is a handover: acids pass protons to bases, reducing agents pass electrons to oxidising agents. Find the giver and the taker and the equation follows. Water's own odd habits, like ice floating, come from hydrogen bonds between its molecules.

Your power bank is full and your phone is flat. One side holds what the other is missing.

Plug in and charge flows from full to empty. In water, some handovers run both ways and settle at a balance.

The phone fills only because the bank drains. What the taker gains, the giver gave up.

what you leave with

five things, not forty.

  • Reactivity is compared by how vigorously metals react with water, dilute acid and oxygen: faster fizzing or brighter burning means the metal is oxidised more readily.
  • Only metals above hydrogen in the series release H₂ gas from dilute acid, e.g. Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g); copper and silver do not react.
  • A metal displaces the ions of any less reactive metal from solution, e.g. Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), so a well-plate grid ranks the metals.
  • Stacking results from all four tests builds an activity series, Ca > Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag, which you then compare with the standard series from a data book.
  • Every one of these reactions is redox: the metal loses electrons (is oxidised), and its place in the series reflects how readily it does so.
